item.title: Exploring student and teacher perspectives on critical thinking with generative AI: early insights from the EduPartnerAI platform
item.description:
Smart Learning Environments
Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has raised important questions about its implications for students’ analytical reasoning and independent judgment. ChatGPT, a generative AI model capable of producing human-like responses, is widely used in academic contexts, yet its educational value requires careful evaluation. This paper presents and evaluates EduPartnerAI, a platform that integrates ChatGPT into student assignments and is designed to encourage critical engagement with AI-generated content. The platform records student-AI interactions, requires students to reflect on ChatGPT’s outputs, and provides teachers with tools to review observable indicators of student reasoning and AI response quality. An exploratory study involving 61 undergraduate students was conducted, relying on student reflection questionnaires, a usability survey, teacher evaluations, and an analysis of recorded interactions. Students generally perceived ChatGPT as a useful learning tool that provided clear explanations and practical examples, although some recognized that its responses could be overly general or incomplete. The teacher observed that students asked relevant questions and effectively incorporated AI-generated content into their assignments but experienced some difficulties with error detection, independent judgment, and critical evaluation. The teacher also judged ChatGPT’s outputs to be largely relevant, clear, and accurate, with few instances of bias or misleading information. Overall, the findings provide preliminary insights into student and teacher perspectives and observable patterns of engagement, highlighting both the educational potential of generative AI and the need for appropriate instructional scaffolding.

item.title: Editrail: Understanding AI Usage by Visualizing Student-AI Interaction in Code
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Programming instructors have diverse philosophies about integrating generative AI into their classes. Some encourage students to use AI, while others restrict or forbid it. Regardless of their approach, all instructors benefit from understanding how their students actually use AI while writing code [1, 14, 25, 38]. Such insight helps instructors assess whether AI use aligns with their pedagogical goals, enables timely intervention when they find unproductive usage patterns, and establishes effective policies for AI use. However, our survey with programming instructors found that many instructors lack visibility into how students use AI in their code-writing processes. To address this challenge, we introduce Editrail, an interactive system that enables instructors to track students’ AI usage, create personalized assessments, and provide timely interventions, all within the workflow of monitoring coding histories. We found that Editrail enables instructors to accurately detect AI use that conflicts with pedagogical goals and to determine when and which students require intervention.

item.title: TeachUp: Facilitating Early-Stage Teachers to Learn Instructional Strategies from Classroom Videos with Reflective Support
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Recorded videos of offline open classes provide good examples for early-stage teachers to learn instructional strategies, e.g., how to organize cooperative learning. However, learning by watching these videos is challenging, as these strategies are implicitly performed, and it lacks in-situ reflective support. In this paper, via a formative study (N=9), we design TeachUp to support the learning of instructional strategies from classroom teaching videos. TeachUp adopts an LLM-powered pipeline to detect nine instructional strategies in videos (precision = 63.4%), provides reflective questions and hints while watching, and generates customized practices with reflective feedback. A within-subjects study (N=16) shows that compared to a traditional video-playing and self-practicing baseline, early-stage teachers with TeachUp are more engaged in learning and perform better in applying learned strategies to new tasks. Interviews with four in-service teachers further generalize our findings and TeachUp’s use cases. We discuss practical implications for fostering video-based learning of instructional strategies.

item.title: Democratizing Extensive Reading by Tailoring Web Content
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Extensive reading helps foreign language learners build proficiency through large amounts of interesting, level-appropriate text. However, providing enough material matched to learners’ interests and evolving proficiency is resource-intensive and difficult to sustain. To address this challenge, we present Adapt-ER, a browser extension that leverages the web to support scalable self-selected reading by adapting pages in place to each learner’s vocabulary profile. Adapt-ER estimates lexical proficiency, tailors web content in real time, and supports lightweight profile refinement through click-based interactive learner feedback during reading. To make adaptation practical during live browsing, we compare LLM-based strategies and develop a hybrid pipeline that balances lexical difficulty control, semantic preservation, latency, and cost. In a within-subject study, Adapt-ER increased reading speed, reduced the need for dictionary and translation support during reading, and improved self-reported engagement. Our findings suggest that in-place adaptation of self-selected web text can make web reading better suited to sustained extensive reading.

item.title: PACEE: Parent-Centered AI Scaffolding for Emotion Education in Early Childhood Conversations
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Emotion education is critical for children aged 3 to 6. However, existing technologies depend substantially on direct child-AI interaction, overlooking the central role of parents in guiding early emotional development at home. To address this gap, we conducted co-design sessions with five kindergarten teachers and five parents to identify key parental challenges and opportunities for AI support in family emotion education. Based on these insights, we developed PACEE, an LLM-based assistant designed around an asymmetric triadic interaction framework: AI primarily supports parents while preserving parent-child interaction. PACEE provides parent-centered AI scaffolding that supports parents in real-time conversation through personalized guidance, post-hoc reflection through trackable feedback, and understanding children’s emotional states through modeling. We evaluated PACEE with 16 families. Results showed that PACEE increased parent-child conversational engagement and improved parents’ overall experience when guiding emotion-related conversations. Together, we contribute an asymmetric triadic interaction framework for AI-supported family education, offering design insights for AI systems that support parents while preserving parent-led parent–child interaction.

item.title: Explorable Proofs: Making Written Proofs Explorable by Grounding Them in Formal Representations
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
LLM-generated explanations can make technical content more accessible, but there is a ceiling on what they can support interactively. Because LLM outputs are static text, they cannot be executed, tinkered with, or stepped through. In this paper, we explore how grounding explanations in a formalized representation enables interactive affordances beyond what static text supports. We instantiate this idea for mathematical proof comprehension in explorable proofs, an approach that uses LLMs to translate a theorem and its written proof into Lean, a programming language for machine-checked proofs, and links the written proof with the Lean code. Readers can work through the proof at a step-level granularity, test custom examples or counterexamples, and trace the logical dependencies bridging between steps. Each worked-out step is produced by executing the Lean proof on an example and extracting its intermediate state. A user study (n = 16) shows potential advantages of this approach: in a proof-understanding task, participants who used the explorability features wrote proof descriptions that an instructor preferred over those written with a proof-and-chatbot baseline, and gave more correct and more detailed answers to proof comprehension questions.

item.title: Interactively Teaching Collaborative Physical Tasks to Generative AI with Narrated Demonstrations
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Enabling users to teach computers how to perform physical tasks is a long-standing goal in HCI. Prior work has explored learning from demonstration, but demonstrations often underspecify intent. Advances in generative AI enable a combination of demonstration and verbal narration to disambiguate intent. However, it remains largely unexplored how to design interfaces that leverage such narrated demonstrations to teach collaborative physical tasks. To probe this design space, we present a prototype system, Apprento, that models physical tasks as programs via generative AI with three integrated interfaces: (1) a teaching interface for providing narrated demonstrations in mixed reality, (2) an inspection interface for visualizing generated programs as decision-flow diagrams and program executions, and (3) a correction interface for iteratively refining generated programs. Across these interfaces, narrated demonstrations serve as a communication modality between users and the system. In a study with 20 participants teaching soccer skills, we identify differing user expectations around authoring and teaching collaborative tasks, as well as key design tensions between task complexity and program interpretability, and between program expressivity and accuracy. We discuss implications for designing future systems that support symbolic modeling of collaborative physical tasks through narrated demonstrations.

item.title: Who's Keeping Score? Interactive Steering of LLM-Powered Scoring with Attune
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to score text records at scale (e.g., rating candidate resumes on a 1–5 scale). However, existing LLM-powered approaches do not account for the fact that effective scoring requires both holistic understanding of records and locally consistent judgments across similar ones. We present Attune, a mixed-initiative system for steerable LLM-powered scoring. Given a task description and scoring range, Attune performs pairwise comparisons across records to develop a global understanding first, and then resolves these comparisons into consistent score assignments—deriving scoring criteria and rules bottom-up in the process. These serve as shared representations of scoring logic that users can inspect and edit. Based on insights from a formative study (n = 12), Attune’s interface introduces novel steering interactions that allow users to deterministically refine scoring logic. Users can provide examples, directly edit criteria, rules, or target distributions, and give natural language feedback—with all refinements compiling into constraints that guide re-scoring. We validate our approach through a technical evaluation across three workloads and a user study with domain experts (n = 8) in healthcare, law, education, and AI evaluation.

item.title: MAIC-UI: Making Interactive Courseware with Generative UI
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Creating interactive STEM courseware traditionally requires HTML/CSS/JavaScript expertise, leaving barriers for educators. While generative AI can produce HTML codes, existing tools generate static presentations rather than interactive simulations, struggle with long documents, and lack pedagogical accuracy mechanisms. Furthermore, full regeneration for modifications requires 200–600 seconds, disrupting creative flow. We present MAIC-UI, a zero-code authoring system that enables educators to create and rapidly edit interactive courseware from textbooks, PPTs, and PDFs. MAIC-UI employs: (1) structured knowledge analysis with multi-modal understanding to ensure pedagogical rigor; (2) a two-stage generate-verify-optimize pipeline separating content alignment from visual refinement; and (3) Click-to-Locate editing with Unified Diff-based incremental generation achieving sub-10-second iteration cycles. A controlled lab study with 40 participants shows MAIC-UI reduces editing iterations (4.9 vs. 7.0) and significantly improves learnability and controllability compared to direct Text-to-HTML generation. A three-month classroom deployment with 53 high school students demonstrates that MAIC-UI fosters learning agency and reduces outcome disparities—the pilot class achieved 9.21-point gains in STEM subjects compared to -2.32 points in control classes. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-MAIC/MAIC-UI.

item.title: CinemaWorld: Generative Augmented Reality with LLMs and 3D Scene Generation for Movie Augmentation
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
We introduce CinemaWorld, a generative augmented reality system that augments the viewer’s physical surroundings with automatically generated mixed reality 3D content extracted from and synchronized with 2D movie scenes. Our system preprocesses films to extract key features using multimodal large language models (LLMs), generates dynamic 3D augmentations with generative AI, and embeds them spatially into the viewer’s physical environment on the Meta Quest 3. To identify key augmentation techniques for CinemaWorld, we conducted an elicitation study with eight film students, which led us to identify several key augmentation types, including particle effects, surrounding objects, textural overlays, character-driven augmentation, and lighting effects. We evaluated our system through a technical evaluation (N=100 video clips), a user evaluation (comparison study: N=12 and in-the-wild study: N=8), and expert interviews with film creators (N=8). Results indicate that CinemaWorld enhances immersion and enjoyment, suggesting its potential to enrich the film-viewing experience.

item.title: TailorCoPilot: Enabling Agentic Pattern Making with Version-Controlled State Tracking
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Experience-driven manufacturing, such as garment pattern making, faces a severe generational skills gap because its core expertise relies on undocumented tacit knowledge forged through day-to-day practice. To address this challenge, we present TailorCoPilot, an agentic pattern-making system built upon a specially designed version-control backend TailorTrace. TailorTrace models sewing patterns as structured, discrete states and records their transformations during the pattern-making process as explicit operation sequences defined upon the geometry primitives in the sewing pattern (panels, edges, vertices and stitches). Integrated into a conventional pattern-making GUI, TailorTrace enables seamless documentation of senior experts’ tacit pattern-making knowledge without breaking their daily workflow. The documented knowledge further offers interactive, pedagogical scaffolding for novices, while providing a robust foundation to power TailorCoPilot and train future generative AI models. In a user study with novices and advanced novices, TailorCoPilot improved task completion rates, reduced time and perceived workload, and yielded higher-quality artifacts compared to skill-appropriate baselines. Ultimately, TailorCoPilot demonstrates a viable pathway to capture practice-based expertise, operationalizing it to support both generative AI advancements and human apprenticeship.

item.title: PATHWiSE: Empowering Teachers with a Generative AI Authoring System for Personalized Robot-Assisted Learning
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Homework assignments often lack the personalized guidance and social interaction crucial for learning. Social robots offer a promising way to bring personalization and interactive support into learning activities; however, teachers rarely have the technical expertise needed to operate robots, let alone create or customize robot-assisted learning (RAL) lessons. To address this challenge, we introduce PATHWiSE, a robust, no-code authoring system designed to empower teachers to create custom RAL activities. Developed through participatory co-design activities with middle school science teachers and students and iteratively refined through multiple user studies, PATHWiSE enables educators to author, preview, and personalize RAL activities that can be tailored to different robot platforms and delivered with either in-person or on-screen robots. The system maintains a flexible trigger-action programming model to define robot expressions contextually related to lesson materials. Through integrated teacher- and student-facing portals, teachers can deploy RAL lessons using a lightweight and portable browser-based approach that affords integration with a wide range of systems. AI-assisted comment and emotion-expression generation tools augment teacher lesson creation while preserving teacher autonomy and expertise in content design. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of PATHWiSE, including its authoring workflow, interface architecture, backend integration, and representative use cases drawn from iterative studies to illustrate the capabilities of the full system.

item.title: As effective as the teacher, but less motivating: a randomized controlled comparison of AI-generated and teacher feedback on students’ writing performance and intrinsic motivation
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers scalable feedback on student writing; however, its effects on writing performance and motivation relative to teacher feedback remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on Feedback Intervention Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this study examined the comparative effectiveness of AI-generated and teacher-provided feedback on students’ writing performance and motivational outcomes. Methods A randomized controlled study assigned 312 undergraduate students to one of three conditions: AI-generated feedback, teacher feedback, or a control condition without substantive feedback. A total of 287 participants were included in the analyses. The study evaluated revised-essay quality, feedback engagement, writing self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, perceived relatedness to the feedback source, and AI literacy. Results Both AI-generated feedback and teacher feedback produced higher revised-essay quality than the control condition, with effect sizes of d = 0.60 and d = 0.59, respectively. The two feedback conditions were statistically equivalent within a prespecified equivalence margin of ±0.35 standard deviations. Feedback engagement, but not writing self-efficacy, statistically accounted for the observed performance advantage. Teacher feedback elicited higher intrinsic motivation than AI-generated feedback, although AI-generated feedback also yielded higher intrinsic motivation than the control condition. This motivational difference was associated with perceived relatedness to the feedback source. The indirect effects identified in the analyses are associational rather than causal. AI literacy did not significantly moderate the effect of feedback on writing performance ( p = 0.058). Discussion Within the context of a single feedback-and-revision cycle at one institution, the findings suggest that AI-generated feedback can achieve writing-performance outcomes comparable to those of teacher feedback, while providing weaker motivational support. These results highlight the potential value of blended feedback approaches that combine the scalability of AI-generated feedback with the relational and motivational strengths of teacher–student interaction. Further research across multiple institutions and repeated feedback cycles is needed to establish the generalizability and longer-term implications of these findings.

item.title: Making argumentative work visible in GenAI-mediated assessment: an exploratory LLM simulation and questionnaire study in university ideological and political education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative AI weakens the correspondence between the final text of an assignment and the argumentative work involved in producing it. This study examined how task structure and AI-use instructions shape evidence use, engagement with objections, and revision in university ideological and political education. Methods An LLM simulation crossed three task formats—position essays, evidence-integration memoranda, and follow-up-and-revision defense tasks—with three AI-use scenarios—simulated no-AI, responsible collaboration, and concealed ghostwriting. Two raters coded 148 generated texts with the Textual Response Artifact Scoring Index (TRASI), and an anonymous questionnaire collected 268 evaluations of 27 selected texts. Results Responsible collaboration produced the highest overall rubric score ( M = 3.32). Evidence-integration memoranda ( M = 3.16) and follow-up-and-revision defenses ( M = 3.10) exceeded position essays ( M = 2.63). Position essays varied most across the three AI-use scenarios, whereas the memorandum and defense showed narrower differences because their instructions already required source explanation or response and revision. Questionnaire participants distinguished the same task functions: memoranda were rated highest for source–claim linkage, and defenses for counterargument response and revision explanation. Open-ended responses associated evidence integration, comparison of reasons, and revision with thinking, while formulaic structure, over-polished expression, and generic abstraction were associated with AI-like writing. Discussion Task structure and AI-use instructions were functionally complementary. Structured tasks elicited source explanation or challenge and revision directly, so responsible collaboration added its largest contribution in the general position essay. GenAI-mediated assessment can therefore be designed around the argumentative decisions that writers are required to document.

item.title: From Narrative to Intent Schema Architecture: An Artificial Intelligence System for Human-Centered Advising Decision Support
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Transfer advising is a high-uncertainty setting where students rarely ask well-structured questions and advisors must infer intent from fragmented narratives across conflicting institutional policies. This research presents a human-centered AI framework that transforms naturalistic student discourse into structured advising intents, supporting a student-facing advising assistant whose explainable outputs are designed to support advisor review. Using 19,668 transfer-related Reddit posts, it surfaces recurring advising intents via extraction, clustering, and structured labeling, then routes student questions to them. On a proof-of-concept benchmark it reached 90% intent-level and 86% question-level accuracy, turning advising knowledge into transparent structures that support scalable, human-centered advising.
